articles.title: Mothers and fathers may pass along different kinds of sexism to their kids, new research suggests
articles.summary: Fathers higher in hostile sexism tended to have children who agreed more with hostile statements about women, while mothers higher in benevolent sexism tended to have children who agreed more that women need men’s protection.

articles.title: Two styles of meditation eased depressive symptoms in a four-week trial, possibly through different routes
articles.summary: Not all meditation may work the same way. In a trial of 147 adults, focused-attention and self-inquiry meditation produced similar drops in depressive symptoms, but exploratory analyses pointed to different underlying processes.

articles.title: The World Won't Wait: Evaluating and Teaching Agents Under a Live Clock
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.20665v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can solve complex interactive tasks, yet reasoning and tool calls take time. In continuously changing environments, an otherwise correct action may arrive too late. We introduce RealtimeBench, with 180 tasks across six game types, to evaluate agents while games continue running during inference. Paired evaluations show that GPT-6.1-sol outperforms the faster Jev when games are paused, but falls behind when they keep running. articles.title: Evaluating Model Capabilities After Benchmark Saturation
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.20667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid advances in AI capabilities are causing benchmarks to saturate. Once several models approach perfect scores, a benchmark loses its power to differentiate between them, and with it its utility for informing AI safety cases and frontier policies. Yet benchmark items produce far more information than the scores we typically extract from them: a full transcript of how each model solved the task. articles.title: Weaker inputs to a key emotion hub are linked to more depressive symptoms in healthy young adults
articles.summary: Young adults with weaker incoming connections to the subgenual anterior cingulate cortex, a small region that helps regulate emotion, tended to report more depressive symptoms, according to brain scans of 890 healthy volunteers.

articles.title: AlphaDiana: A Measurement System for Agents in Verifiable Reasoning Tasks
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.20675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents pair reasoning models with harnesses that organize model calls, execute tools, load skill instructions, and retain history in memory. Understanding agent performance requires linking execution conditions to outcomes, behavior, and resource use. We introduce AlphaDiana, a measurement system with modular interfaces for datasets, agents, environments, and scorers. It preserves harness-native control loops while controlling file reuse and memory retention separately. AlphaDiana supports macro analyses of complete agents and micro interventions

articles.title: Frontiers: A Roundtable Discussion on the I-Frame vs. S-Frame Debate
articles.summary: Applied behavioral scientists believe their work can influence people’s lives for the better. But what is the most effective way to make that happen? Is it through interventions focused on influencing individual behavior while maintaining freedom of choice? Is it by changing policies and laws, and thereby the systems, that individuals operate within? Is it a combination of the two? Is the distinction between an individual- or systems-focus a helpful one? Or, is the world too messy and complex? How should applied behavioral scientists navigate the financial and political influences on the work

articles.title: Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness
articles.summary: Even under general anesthesia, the human brain can analyze language, recognize different types of words, and predict what comes next in a story, according to a surprising discovery by Baylor researchers. The findings challenge our understanding of consciousness and suggest that the unconscious brain is far more capable than scientists previously realized.

articles.summary: A large study reveals that unhealthy habits like excessive screen time and poor diet tend to group together in teenagers. These behavioral clusters strongly predict the future onset of combined anxiety and depression.

articles.summary: Highly intelligent women often face a hidden social penalty in the workplace. A new study reveals that female employees with high cognitive ability are perceived as more hostile, leading to fewer supportive interactions with their colleagues.

articles.title: Learning to read may shape how adults reason about what others believe
articles.summary: Can learning to read change how we think about other people’s minds? Among 76 Turkish women, reading fluency was the strongest predictor of performance on a test of reasoning about what one person thinks another believes.

articles.title: Weak handgrip strength linked to higher risk of depression over time
articles.summary: A massive new review of medical data reveals that lower handgrip strength is linked to a higher risk of developing depression over time, suggesting physical strength may serve as an early indicator of general health and mental vulnerability.

articles.title: Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered a surprising two-way relationship between sleep and growth hormone, revealing how the brain carefully balances physical recovery with wakefulness. The findings could help explain why poor sleep harms metabolism and brain health, potentially opening the door to new treatments for sleep and neurological disorders.

articles.title: Brain cells meant to protect us may be fueling cognitive decline
articles.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising cause of age-related cognitive decline involving brain cells previously thought to be entirely beneficial. As these cells become dysfunctional, they can produce abnormal amounts of myelin, disrupting nerve fibers and potentially contributing to worsening memory and thinking skills.

articles.title: How public opinion on transgender bathroom access shifted between 2016 and 2022
articles.summary: Public opinion on transgender bathroom access has grown more conservative since 2016. A new study reveals how Americans weigh competing arguments about safety and discrimination, and why conflicted voters increasingly support restrictive policies.

articles.title: Nostalgia for a party’s past cuts both ways when it comes to support for political violence
articles.summary: Nostalgia for a party’s past doesn’t mean the same thing to every partisan. Partisans who felt nostalgic reported more support for violence if their passion was obsessive, but less if it was harmonious.

articles.title: New compounds target clumping enzyme to protect brain cells in Alzheimer’s models
articles.summary: An enzyme called GRK2 clumps up and damages cellular powerhouses in the brains of mice with Alzheimer's disease. Newly developed chemical compounds that prevent or eliminate these clumps helped preserve memory and slow brain cell death in the animals.
